title: NMR: how many signals, and what a multiplet tells you
asks: A structure is given. Say how many proton or carbon signals it shows, or what a splitting pattern reveals.

know.h: In spectroscopy a sample absorbs specific frequencies of light, and those frequencies tell us the structure. The energy absorbed, hν, equals the gap between a lower and a higher energy state.

Each proton is a tiny magnet. In an external magnetic field most are aligned with the field (lower energy) and some against it (higher energy). The gap between the two grows as the field {{B0}} gets stronger.
There are two kinds to know: {{1H}} NMR looks at the hydrogens, {{13C}} NMR looks at the carbons.
Shielding: electrons have their own magnetic field, which counters the external field. The nucleus feels a net field of {{B0}} minus the electrons' field.

An electronegative atom pulls electron density away from the hydrogens near it, so they are less shielded and feel a larger net field. In fluoroethane the {{CH2}} next to F and the {{CH3}} are in different environments.
One signal for each different environment. Nuclei in the same environment (equivalent nuclei) share a signal. Fluoroethane: two {{1H}} signals and two {{13C}} signals.
The three hydrogens of a {{CH3}} are always equivalent, because the group spins. The two hydrogens of a {{CH2}} in an open chain are equivalent in the molecules of this course.
Groups that are swapped by a mirror plane or by turning the molecule around are equivalent: the two {{CH3}} groups of propane or acetone give one signal.
A double bond does not rotate. In bromoethene all three hydrogens are different: three signals.
Resonance can make atoms equivalent: the two end {{CH2}} groups of the allyl cation are the same, and the middle CH is different.
The n + 1 rule: a hydrogen with n equivalent hydrogens on the next carbon appears as n + 1 lines. 0 neighbours: singlet. 1: doublet. 2: triplet. 3: quartet. 6: septet.
Patterns to recognize: an ethyl group is a triplet (3 H) and a quartet (2 H). An isopropyl group is a doublet (6 H) and a septet (1 H). A tert-butyl or isolated {{CH3}} group is a singlet.
Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other, and a carbon with no hydrogens still gives a {{13C}} signal.

method: Draw the structure with every hydrogen (or number every carbon).
Look for symmetry: a mirror plane, two identical ends, or resonance that makes atoms the same.
Group the atoms into environments. Atoms swapped by symmetry, and the hydrogens of one {{CH3}}, go in the same group.
Count the groups: that is the number of signals.
For splitting, pick one group of hydrogens, count the hydrogens on the directly attached carbons (n), and write n + 1 lines.
To read a multiplet backwards, subtract one from the number of lines to get the number of neighbours, then ask which group has that many.

pitfalls.h: Counting hydrogens, or counting groups, instead of environments: propane has eight hydrogens and three carbons but two {{1H}} signals.
Missing symmetry, so that equivalent groups are counted twice.
Using the hydrogens' own number in the n + 1 rule. The rule counts the neighbours.
Treating the two hydrogens of a ={{CH2}} as equivalent when the other end of the double bond carries two different groups.
Leaving out carbons with no hydrogens (C=O, a ring carbon carrying a group) when counting {{13C}} signals.
